There's a paradigm of educational thought that sometimes gets called the 'Standardized Management Paradigm' by curriculum scholars. This is the paradigm that more or less ruled the public school system of most developed countries from the post-world-war era until very recently (and reigns supreme in many places still). The Standardized Management Paradigm is based off the industrial model which assumes that children, just like machinery, are completely interchangeable and can all be taught the exact same thing in the exact same way. Any deviation from the expected outcomes is presumed to be a failure on the part of the student, not on the part of the teaching method, curriculum, or any of the systemic factors involved. Differing from the expected norm is considered a bad thing, a defect. It promotes conformity and punishes creativity and expression. Under this model, the curriculum is a pre-determined thing that is presumed to be known in its entirety and is taught to a captive audience of children who are presumed to have no knowledge or ability of their own and are just there to passively absorb the 'thing' that is the curriculum. Once again, this is the model that has prevailed in much of the developed world, and still prevails intensely in a lot of places. It produces nice little cogs who know how to follow instructions but can't think for themselves or problem solve. They can handle textbook situations but nothing more advanced than that, because it's heavily compartmentalized and there's not a lot of interdisciplinary collaboration. In fact, interdisciplinary collaboration is discouraged in a kind of academic subject fence pissing match which considers only those disciplines valuable to STEM to be worthy of note. Anything involving human experience is systematically devalued in favour of STEM subjects.

The good news is that there are other forms of thought in curriculum design, such as Curricular Wisdom. Curricular Wisdom is incredibly effective at getting kids engaged, learning, and thinking critically about information, and it doesn't penalize the non-conformists like Standardized Management does. It's not predicated on a teacher-as-a-master model but on a teacher-as-a-collaborator. The problem with Curricular Wisdom and other similar humanistic models is that it's labour intensive for the teacher - it requires that the teacher be trained in the paradigm (most teachers were educated in the Standardized Management Paradigm and thus mindlessly repeat the Standardized Management Paradigm), deeply internalize the values, and spend the time to plan curricula under this paradigm. Applying it in the classroom is difficult to do with a large class or in an underfunded classroom.

The ballooning class sizes, underfunded education system, overworked, underpaid teaching staff, and lack of support staff are no mere oversight or error. It's a deliberately designed setup that basically guarantees that the only possible teaching style will be Standardized Management, because it can be easily churned out and mass produced and fits well with standardized testing. It ensures that those who are deemed as valid of entry into society in general are all trained in exactly the same way with exactly the same narrow range of opinions and thoughts, and that those who 'fail to conform' to the standard remain marginalized throughout their lives. Applying something that works, like Curriculum Wisdom, and that actually benefits learners, on a national or even district scale would cost money, resources, and require that we respect teaching as a profession and support teachers a lot more than we do. It would also require significant retraining of the current teaching staff. For stressed out, underpaid teachers with little support, the only easily available tools they can reach for and keep using year after year are Standardized Management tools. Standardized Management virtually ensures its own continuance, and is also easily manipulated by a few interests setting the 'standards' for curricula.

This summer I will begin a series on the basics of bartending. Any and all contribution is welcome, and for those with better or different information, feel free to chime in.

Part 1: Bartending Terminology

Back - a small glass of juice, soda, or water which accompanies a drink.

Bar Spoon - A long mixing spoon; often having a lemon zester or muddler at the other end.

Bitters - An herbal cocktail flavoring

Blend - To mix up ingredients in a blender, drinks using this method are called blended or frozen.

Build - A term for the method of making a drink: starting with ice, and building the drink by adding ingredients in order.

Call Drink - When a customer orders a drink by giving the specific liquor and mixer.

Chaser - Anything that is consumed directly following the taking of a straight shot, or shooter.

Chill - To chill a glass, add ice and water (or soda water,) to any glass and let it sit while you mix the drink. Often used for Martinis.

Cocktail - A mix of alcohol, liqueur, and mixer.

Dash - A few drops of an ingredient.

Dirty - To make a Martini “dirty,” add olive juice. The more, the dirtier.

Dry - The use of dry vermouth, most often for a Martini, or Manhattan.

Float - Used for layered drinks, you would float a lighter alcohol on top of a denser alcohol: (E.g. a B-52 shooter contains Kahlua, Irish Cream and Grand Marnier. Kahlua is heavier than Irish Cream which is heavier than GM so each one floats on the other. This can be done by pouring very carefully down the side of the glass or pouring the floated alcohol over an inverted spoon, allowing the alcohol to trickle off the spoon in many directions)

Free Pour - To make and mix drinks without using a bar’s measuring device (jigger.) Garnish - Typically fruit, a garnish is something added to a drink after it’s mixed to enhance presentation and give additional flavoring options.

Highball - Liquor mixed with soda, served in a tall glass (often called a highball glass.)

Jigger - A jigger is an hour-glass shaped measuring device - most often one side is 1oz(30ml)(a standard shot pour.

Layer - Layering is the same as floating. The heavier alcohol goes on the bottom, and the next lighter alcohol is layered on top using a careful pour over an inverted spoon. Most bars have a spoon designed specifically for layering, not the same as the bar spoon.

Mixer - Mixers are the non-alcoholic additions to cocktails and mixed drinks. (Water, Juice, Soda, etc.)

Muddle - To crush up ingredients, such as a mint, or fruit, using the bar tool called a muddler.

Neat - A shot poured directly out of the bottle. No ice.

Pony - A pony, or a pony shot is equal to 1oz of liquor.

Premium/Top Shelf - Typically more expensive, but specifically higher quality liquor. (Grey Goose, Tanqueray, etc.)

Rim - To rim a glass, first wet the rim of the glass with lime juice, then press the rim into your rimmer of choice: Salt, Sugar, Celery Salt, etc.

Rocks (On the) - Simply refers to a drink with ice.

Roll - Pouring a mixed drink gently into and out of a cocktail shaker. Whereas Boxing is a quick hard shake of the drink.

Shaker Tin (cocktail shaker) - A bar tool, most often metal, used to shake all the ingredients in a mixed drink together.

Strain - Using a bar strainer to pour only the liquid ingredients into a drink, after having been shaken with ice, squeezed fruit, etc.

Shooter - A shot, or shooter, is a 1-2oz serving of either straight liquor, or with additional mixers, meant to be drank in a single gulp.

Sour - Refers to the sourness of Lime Sour, Sweet & Sour, Margarita Mix - all variations of the same thing, used as a mixer in different cocktails. (Whiskey Sour)

Speed Rail - A long stainless steel shelf convenient to the bartender’s location, containing the most commonly ordered liquors, often well liquors.

Straight up - A drink shaken with ice, that is strained into a glass. Martinis use this method.

Twist - A garnish using the rind of a citrus fruit.

Virgin - A non-alcoholic version of popular cocktails. Also known as a mocktail.

Well Liquor/Well Drink - In most bars, a lower quality liquor used for basic highball style drinks. (e.g. rum & coke)

I'm curious about the large scale investments. Hosting a community, especially as it grows quickly isn't free. The investments can take care of the short term but ultimately Voat will need some stable source of income to continue to grow and expand over time. I'm not sure how feasible it is to host a community like this long term simply through donations. I would imagine some form of advertising or membership benefits would help to bring in the income. But at what level would that become a stable enough source of income to maintain Voat and keep it afloat?

Yes, of course you are correct in suggesting they cannot survive purely on the pure donations and investments alone. I would expect them to use advertisements as one revenue stream which comes with benefits and drawbacks. Before they start investing in higher end infrastructure they need to sit down and determine how they will pay for it month to month past the initial bomb cost which would hopefully be covered by investments now. Even advertisements are not going to be enough to fund the site so they will need to supplements them with some incentive for people to donate. How they incentivise the donations is important because they need to find a balance that doesn't make people feel cheated if they don't have the ability to pay. It's going to be interesting how they choose to handle it to say the least.

It was more a here and there thing to donate a little back to the site I was spending much of my time at. Even then, I never felt like I was losing out on anything whether I was subscribed or not.
